===== ORIGINAL PROMPT (initial_prompt.md) =====
Build a native iOS Solitaire (Klondike) game — SwiftUI, 100% local, zero
network calls, zero sign-in/accounts/analytics/telemetry of any kind. No
backend. All state (stats, settings, saved game) persists on-device only.

THE CENTRAL CONSTRAINT — READ THIS FIRST: this must be a real, fully
playable, correctly-rules-implemented Klondike solitaire game. Drag-and-drop
(or tap-to-move) card interaction, legal-move validation, win detection,
undo, new-game/deal, and a stock/waste/foundation/tableau layout that
actually works. Do not let the visual ambition come at the cost of the game
being playable and correct — a beautiful app that can't be played is a
failure.

VISUAL DESIGN — THIS IS THE PART THAT MUST WIN AWARDS:
Cards must look like real, tactile playing cards — not the generic flat
rounded-rectangles-with-tiny-corner-pips that every solitaire clone uses.
Invent a genuinely original custom card face system: bespoke rank/suit
typography or iconography (not SF Symbols reused as suit glyphs), a
consistent illustrated or generative pattern language across all 52 cards
and the card back, real card-stock texture/shadow/lighting, and satisfying
physical motion (cards should feel like they have weight — spring-based
drag, believable flip/deal animation, subtle parallax or depth).

The bar: this should look and feel like something from an Apple Design
Award reel, not a tutorial app. Judge yourself against that bar throughout
— if a screen looks like a stock SwiftUI solitaire tutorial, it has failed
the brief. One clear, original visual "hook" (an art direction, a material
language, a signature interaction) should be identifiable in one glance
that no other solitaire app has.

Also include: light/dark mode (both fully art-directed, not just inverted
colors), haptics on card moves/wins, a stats screen (games played/won,
best time, streak — all local), and a settings screen (draw-1 vs draw-3,
card back selection, timer on/off).

Ship something that could realistically be submitted to the App Store today
and be visually distinctive in a screenshot alone.

## Final Output

Okay, I want to actually sit with Codex's "gesture/z-order debt" phrase instead of gliding past it, because on reflection I think I was underweighting exactly what "drag" costs beyond the validation call. I framed it in round 2 as "drag is just a thin layer that calls the same `attemptMove` function tap already uses" — and that's true for the *decision* of whether a move is legal, but it's not true for the *engineering* around it. Live drag means continuous touch tracking, dynamically recomputing and highlighting legal drop targets as the finger moves across the board (not just once at drop, the way tap can), and doing that hit-testing with the extra padding beyond visual card bounds that product_research already flagged as necessary because the tableau columns are narrow. That's real, standalone surface area — it's not "the same correctness core with a coat of paint," it's a second interaction pipeline with its own bug class (mid-drag z-order, drop-zone ambiguity when two columns are close together, gesture cancellation mid-flight). Codex is right that bolting that onto a slice whose entire purpose is proving the rules engine is stable is a distraction from the actual test, not a free addition to it.

So here's where I land, and I think this actually gives both of us what we care about instead of either of us just caving: slice 1 ships tap-to-move only as the interaction *model* — no live finger-tracking, no drop-zone hit-testing, no continuous gesture state. But I want it on record that "tap-to-move" cannot quietly mean "cards teleport." When a tap resolves to a legal move, the card's transit to its destination has to be a real spring-physics animation — lift off the pile with a little weight to it, travel with a spring curve, settle onto the target with an actual bounce/settle, not a linear slide or a cross-dissolve. That's the part of "spring-based... cards should feel like they have weight" from the original prompt that I don't want to lose just because we're deferring live drag, because it's cheap to build (it's an animation curve on a state transition we're already implementing) and it's the difference between "correct" and "feels like the app the brief is asking for." Deferring live interactive drag to increment 2 also has a nice side effect: it bundles the whole hit-testing/drop-zone problem together with multi-card run-drag in one later increment, instead of us solving half of that problem now (single-card hit-testing) and half later (multi-card), which is a more coherent way to sequence it than what I was originally proposing.

On the stats-recording wrinkle — Codex, you didn't object to it and the coordinator flagged it as still technically unconfirmed, so let me just make the actual case plainly so we can close it: this is not a feature, it's a data-loss prevention measure that costs nothing. If slice 1 is genuinely going to be played by anyone — even just us, dogfooding it — the moment a Stats screen exists in increment 2, someone's going to want to know "how many games have I played since I started using this," and if we didn't record anything during slice 1, the honest answer is "we don't know," which is a weird thing to ship in an app whose entire pitch is "we tell you the truth about your own data, unlike the freemium apps." It's a struct appended to local storage on game-start/game-end events, no UI, no settings dependency, nothing that risks the correctness surface we're trying to protect. I'd like this confirmed as a real decision, not left as an unresolved footnote.

So, to state where I think this fully lands now, three-for-three: no Settings/Stats UI in slice 1, but real game-event data recorded silently to local storage from day one; a real, non-placeholder deal/flip animation with actual spring sequencing and real card art; and tap-to-move as the only interaction model in slice 1, with the requirement that the tap-resolved move itself animates with genuine spring/weight physics rather than a flat instant placement, and live interactive drag (single-card and multi-card both) deferred together as their own later increment. I think that's a slice that's honest about what it's testing — rules correctness, persistence integrity, the deal-animation hook, and whether spring-physics motion reads as premium — without pretending we've de-risked drag interaction when we haven't even started it yet.

## Final Output

**Architecture overview.** Single Xcode target, no dynamic frameworks. One `@MainActor @Observable GameEngine` is the sole mutable-state owner (board, interaction, timer), instantiated once at the App root and injected via `@Environment`. Its production `newGame` always defaults to the system RNG; the `rng` parameter is a test-only seam that must never be reachable from any UI/Settings surface ([REDACTED:high_entropy]). Domain types have zero SwiftUI imports and zero dependency on the persistence layer, which itself only knows `Codable` structs — this boundary is what keeps parallel build lanes decoupled.

**File/module layout:** `App/` (entry point, root `TabView`, service wiring), `DesignSystem/` (`Theme.swift` token source + `CardGlyphs/` bespoke `Shape` library), `Domain/` (pure value types, `GameEngine`, `StuckDetector` implementations, `RestoreIntegrityService` — fully unit-testable with no view hierarchy), `Persistence/` (three file stores, `AtomicFileWriter`, `AppRestoreCoordinator`), `Features/Game/`, `Features/Stats/`, `Features/Settings/`, `Interaction/` (`HapticsService`, gesture glue), `DebugTools/` (`#if DEBUG` legibility gallery).

**Data models.** `Card` has no stored `id` — it's computed from `suit`+`rank` (`"\(rank.rawValue)\(suit.rawValue)"`), guaranteed unique under the locked single-deck rule, stable across `isFaceUp` toggling (so it keys `matchedGeometryEffect` correctly through a flip), and structurally excluded from `Codable` round-tripping since it's never a stored field. `PileID.foundation` is `Suit`-keyed, not `Int`-keyed, so "one foundation per suit" is a compile-time fact. `GameState` is pure logical board state only — no undo history, no animation/selection fields; the undo stack lives exclusively in `GameSaveFile` as a capped-200 LIFO full-state log (`popLast()`, no redo — nothing in this pipeline ever asked for redo). `InteractionState` is the single named FSM the Game screen reads from instead of scattered `@State` booleans. Stuck detection is two separate types (`DrawOneStuckDetector` exact, `DrawThreeStuckDetector` conservative) behind one `StuckDetector` protocol, independently fuzz-testable per DEC-app_features-002's differing exactness bar. Stats persist as a two-case event stream (`gameStarted` written immediately at session start, `gameEnded` on completion) so a crashed/abandoned session still shows up as played, with `DrawModeStats` as a derived, incrementally-updated cache rather than a per-render recompute.

**Persistence strategy.** Three independently-atomic-written files (`GameSave.json`, `StatsLog.json`, `Settings.json`), each behind its own actor conforming to one shared `PersistenceStore` protocol, `load()` returning `RestoreOutcome<Model>` directly (`.restored` / `.fallbackDefault` / `.dataLoss`) rather than throwing — this is the type-level enforcement of design_discussion's three-outcome recovery UI requirement. `GameSaveStore.load()` decodes, then runs `RestoreIntegrityService.validate(_:)` as a mandatory semantic gate (52 unique cards, no duplicate/missing ranks-per-suit, legal stacking, foundation monotonicity) before ever exposing a resumed board — a decodable-but-illegal save is `.dataLoss`, never silently activated. Saves are debounced ~300-500ms per store with write-coalescing, plus an unconditional `flush()` on `scenePhase` background. `AppRestoreCoordinator` runs all three loads concurrently and owns the single app-level `hasFinishedInitialLoad` flag that gates first paint across all three tabs.

**Testing strategy.** Unchanged from ios_architecture_review's locked plan (unit tests over legality/win/undo, randomized fuzz simulation per draw mode, XCUITest over observable flows, mandatory accessibility identifiers, `performAccessibilityAudit()`), now sharpened by this phase's types: the fuzz suite can target `DrawOneStuckDetector` and `DrawThreeStuckDetector` independently, and `RestoreIntegrityService` gets its own dedicated corrupt/invalid-save test fixtures.

# iOS HIG + Native UX Cheatsheet (iOS 17+ / SwiftUI)

Rules for building iPhone apps that feel native and premium. Target iOS 17+, Swift 5.9+, SwiftUI-first, zero third-party deps. Snippets are idiomatic and compile on an iOS 17 deployment target unless a newer minimum is called out. When SwiftUI can't do it, drop to UIKit via `UIViewRepresentable`/`UIViewControllerRepresentable` — noted where relevant.

## Core principles (apply to every screen)

- **Prefer system components.** Native controls inherit Dynamic Type, VoiceOver, Reduce Motion, RTL, and dark mode for free. A custom control means you re-implement all of that or ship an inaccessible app.
- **Use semantic colors** (`Color.primary`, `.secondary`, `Color(.systemBackground)`, `.tint`), never hardcoded hex, so light/dark/increase-contrast modes work automatically.
- **Respect safe areas.** Let system spacing (`.padding()` with no argument) and `Spacer()` drive layout; avoid magic pixel numbers.
- **Use text styles** (`.font(.body)`, `.headline`, …), which scale with Dynamic Type. Fixed point sizes don't — avoid them for user-facing text.
- **One primary action per screen.** Everything else is secondary/tertiary in visual weight.
- **Latency budget:** any action >100ms needs feedback (spinner, skeleton, or optimistic UI). A measurable task >1s should show determinate progress.

## Navigation: pick the right container

Decision order — do NOT default to a sheet or a tab bar:

- **Tab bar (`TabView`)**: 2–5 top-level, peer sections the user switches between freely (Home, Search, Profile). Never for a linear flow or steps. Each tab persists its own navigation stack. Don't hide the tab bar mid-flow; if a screen needs full focus, present it modally instead.
- **Navigation stack (`NavigationStack`)**: drill-down into hierarchical content (list → detail → sub-detail). Push when the destination is a child of the current context and the user will want the back button + swipe-back.
- **Sheet (`.sheet`)**: a self-contained, interruptive task the user completes and dismisses (compose, filter, quick edit, share). Use detents for lightweight tasks. A sheet keeps the parent visible behind it — signals "you'll come right back."
- **Full-screen cover (`.fullScreenCover`)**: onboarding, media playback, camera, or a task that demands total focus with no parent context. Use sparingly — it breaks the "come right back" mental model.
- **Alert / confirmationDialog**: a decision, not a task. `alert` = 1–2 choices needing acknowledgment. `confirmationDialog` = a short list of actions (esp. destructive) anchored to what the user tapped.

Rule of thumb: if the user can be "in the middle of it" and navigate away, it's a stack. If they must finish or cancel, it's a sheet/cover. If it's a yes/no, it's an alert.

### NavigationStack with type-safe routing

Prefer value-based navigation over `NavigationLink(destination:)` — it enables deep linking, programmatic pop-to-root, and state restoration.

```swift

    case detail(itemID: UUID)
    case settings
}

    @State private var path: [Route] = []
    let store: ItemStore

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack(path: $path) {
            List(store.items) { item in
                NavigationLink(value: Route.detail(itemID: item.id)) {
                    ItemRow(item: item)
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Items")
            .navigationDestination(for: Route.self) { route in
                switch route {
                case .detail(let id): DetailView(itemID: id)
                case .settings:       SettingsView()
                }
            }
        }
    }

    func popToRoot() { path.removeAll() }
    func openSettings() { path.append(.settings) }
}
```
